```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (Goff and Stafford with the Rams; third-and-long dropbacks, 2019-2025)"
#| output: false
def rams_qb(name, seasons):
    x = DROP[(DROP["passer"] == name) & (DROP["posteam"] == "LA") & DROP["season"].isin(seasons)]
    y = x[(x["down"] == 3) & (x["ydstogo"] >= 7)]
    return x["epa"].mean(), y["epa"].mean()


GOFF_LA, GOFF_T3 = rams_qb("J.Goff", [2017, 2018, 2019, 2020])
STAF_LA, STAF_T3 = rams_qb("M.Stafford", list(range(2021, 2026)))

_d = DROP[(DROP["season"] >= 2019) & (DROP["down"] == 3) & (DROP["ydstogo"] >= 7)]
_t = _d.groupby("posteam")["epa"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
T3_SF, T3_LG, T3_RANK = _t["SF"], _d["epa"].mean(), list(_t.index).index("SF") + 1
_air = _d.groupby("posteam")["air_yards"].mean().rank(ascending=False, method="min")
_yac = _d[_d["complete_pass"] == 1].groupby("posteam")["yards_after_catch"].mean().rank(ascending=False, method="min")
T3_AIR_RK, T3_YAC_RK = int(_air["SF"]), int(_yac["SF"])
```

Read @fig-same-qb with care, because it is the kind of chart that can prove whatever you want. Darnold's
jump from `{python} f"{QB.loc['Sam Darnold', 'epa_out']:+.2f}"` to `{python} f"{QB.loc['Sam Darnold', 'epa_in']:+.2f}"`
EPA per dropback and Mac Jones's from `{python} f"{QB.loc['Mac Jones', 'epa_out']:+.2f}"` to
`{python} f"{QB.loc['Mac Jones', 'epa_in']:+.2f}"` are large, and they happened with new teammates, new
offensive lines and, in Darnold's case, a few more years of experience. Tagovailoa is the cleanest
comparison (same team, same player, a new head coach in 2022), and his line hides a collapse: his 2025 season
under McDaniel was his worst since his rookie year, and McDaniel was fired that winter. Garoppolo's drop after
leaving San Francisco came at age 32 and after injuries. And Goff, traded by McVay to Detroit for Matthew
Stafford in 2021, averaged `{python} f"{QB.loc['Jared Goff', 'epa_out']:+.2f}"` per dropback in Detroit against
`{python} f"{QB.loc['Jared Goff', 'epa_in']:+.2f}"` in Los Angeles, and had his best season (2024) after the Lions built
their own run-and-play-action offense around him. Goff's line doesn't show a limit; it shows that the ideas
travel to a cousin offense.

The Goff-for-Stafford trade is the sharpest test of the "system" argument, and the averages can't settle it.
With the Rams, Goff (2017–2020) averaged `{python} f"{GOFF_LA:+.2f}"` EPA per dropback and Stafford (2021–2025)
`{python} f"{STAF_LA:+.2f}"`; on third down with 7 or more to go, `{python} f"{GOFF_T3:+.2f}"` and
`{python} f"{STAF_T3:+.2f}"`. Yet McVay made the trade, won Super Bowl LVI in Stafford's first season, and in
2025, with Stafford at 37, the Rams led the league in play-action and still had the MVP at quarterback: Stafford
threw a league-leading 46 touchdown passes.[^stafford] Whatever McVay was paying for lives in the handful of
plays an average hides, the ones that decide January games. That is a coach's judgment, not a number, and it's
honest to call it one.

The critics have one more argument: the big games. Kyle Shanahan's offenses have led in the second half of
three Super Bowls and lost all three: as Atlanta's coordinator in Super Bowl LI (up 28–3 in the third quarter,
lost 34–28 in overtime), and as the 49ers' head coach in Super Bowl LIV (up 20–10 in the fourth quarter, lost
31–20) and Super Bowl LVIII (lost 25–22 in overtime).[^sbs] Those losses get pinned on play-calling with a lead
and on an offense that, critics say, can't throw its way out of obvious passing downs. The second claim is
testable, and the data doesn't support it. From 2019 to 2025, on third down with 7 or more yards to go (the
downs where everybody knows it is a pass), the 49ers' dropbacks averaged
`{python} f"{T3_SF:+.2f}"` EPA, `{python} ordinal(T3_RANK)` of 32 teams, against a league average of
`{python} f"{T3_LG:+.2f}"`. Look at *how*, though: their throws travelled less far in the air than most teams'
(`{python} ordinal(T3_AIR_RK)` in average air yards on those snaps) and their completions gained more after the
catch (`{python} ordinal(T3_YAC_RK)` in YAC per catch). Even on third-and-long, the 49ers' answer is designed:
a schemed throw to a receiver on the move, not a quarterback inventing something.

So the honest summary is in between. The system reliably raises the *floor*: quarterbacks who can read a
defense, deliver the ball on time and throw on the move become efficient in it, and some of them have looked
like stars. Its third-and-long numbers say the design reaches further than critics think. What no design
supplies is the throw after the design breaks (the coverage was right, the protection failed, and the
quarterback has to create something), and those plays are rare enough that season averages barely see them.
Whether they decide the biggest games is the real argument, and it is one the data in this chapter can't end.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"System quarterback" means "bad quarterback."** It doesn't, and the phrase is used carelessly in both
directions. Every quarterback plays in a system; the Shanahan system just makes its contribution unusually
visible. Matt Ryan's MVP season (2016), Aaron Rodgers's MVP seasons under Matt LaFleur (2020 and 2021) and
Stafford's in 2025 all came in this family's offenses, from quarterbacks nobody calls system players. The
useful question isn't "system or quarterback?" but "how much does this quarterback add *beyond* what the design
gives him?", which is what EPA, CPOE and YAC over expected try to separate.
:::

## The data fingerprint

How would you recognise this offense from data alone, without watching a snap? Four measurements do most
of the work: how often the quarterback is under center, how often he fakes a handoff, how much the receivers
gain after the catch, and (to check that all this produces anything) how efficient the offense is.

### Under center and play-action

The chart below sorts the 2025 play-callers into two generations. The **first generation** are the coaches who
worked on the Shanahans' or Kubiaks' own staffs and called plays in 2025: Kyle Shanahan (49ers), Sean McVay
(Rams), Matt LaFleur (Packers), Mike McDaniel (Dolphins) and Klint Kubiak (Seahawks); the tree section below
traces how each got there. The **second generation** came up on McVay's Rams staffs: Kevin O'Connell (Vikings),
Zac Taylor (Bengals), Liam Coen (Jaguars), and two coordinators who called plays in 2025, Zac Robinson in
Atlanta and Nick Caley in Houston.[^gen2]

```{python}
#| label: fig-fingerprint
#| fig-cap: "The 2025 fingerprint: how often each offense put the quarterback under center (share of runs and passes) against how often it used play-action (share of dropbacks), from FTN's charting. Dark blue: the five first-generation play-callers (Shanahan, McVay, Matt LaFleur, McDaniel and Klint Kubiak). Green: five play-callers who came up on McVay's Rams staffs. Grey: the rest of the league. The dashed lines are the league medians. Four of the five first-generation teams sit right of the under-center median, the Rams at the far corner of both; McDaniel's Dolphins, the speed-and-motion branch, worked mostly from the shotgun and pistol. The dashed arrow is the one 2024 element: Seattle's move from 2024 to 2025, Klint Kubiak's one season as play-caller. The second generation is spread out: a coaching tree passes on ideas, not a single formula. Data: nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting, regular seasons."
FP_SEASONS = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting(FP_SEASONS).to_pandas()
fp = PLAYS[PLAYS["season"].isin(FP_SEASONS)].merge(
    ftn[["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "qb_location", "is_play_action", "is_motion"]],
    left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"])
fp["uc"] = fp["qb_location"].eq("U")
FP = fp.groupby(["season", "posteam"]).agg(uc=("uc", "mean"), motion=("is_motion", "mean"))
FP = FP.join(fp[fp["qb_dropback"] == 1].groupby(["season", "posteam"]).agg(pa=("is_play_action", "mean")))
for col in ("uc", "pa", "motion"):
    FP[col + "_rk"] = FP.groupby(level="season")[col].rank(ascending=False, method="min").astype(int)
LG_UC = fp.groupby("season")["uc"].mean()

CORE = {"SF": "49ers (Shanahan)", "LA": "Rams (McVay)", "GB": "Packers (LaFleur)",
        "MIA": "Dolphins (McDaniel)", "SEA": "Seahawks (Kubiak)"}
MCVAY = {"MIN": "Vikings", "CIN": "Bengals", "JAX": "Jaguars", "ATL": "Falcons", "HOU": "Texans"}
f25 = FP.xs(2025, level="season")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.3))
rest = f25[~f25.index.isin(list(CORE) + list(MCVAY))]
ax.scatter(rest["uc"], rest["pa"], s=34, color=style.BASELINE, edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.8, zorder=2,
           label="other offenses")
ax.scatter(f25.loc[list(MCVAY), "uc"], f25.loc[list(MCVAY), "pa"], s=46, color=style.SERIES[2],
           edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.8, zorder=3, label="second generation (from McVay's staffs)")
ax.scatter(f25.loc[list(CORE), "uc"], f25.loc[list(CORE), "pa"], s=62, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
           edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.8, zorder=4, label="first generation")
LABEL_OFF = {"SF": (7, -10), "LA": (-6, 8), "GB": (-6, 9), "MIA": (-7, -8), "SEA": (7, 4),
             "MIN": (7, 2), "CIN": (-7, 0), "JAX": (7, -4), "ATL": (7, -6), "HOU": (7, 2)}
LABEL_AT = {"GB": (0.405, 0.292), "MIA": (0.205, 0.292)}     # crowded spots: label in open space, with a leader
for tm, off_ in LABEL_OFF.items():
    lab = CORE.get(tm, MCVAY.get(tm))
    r = f25.loc[tm]
    if tm in LABEL_AT:
        ax.annotate(lab, (r["uc"], r["pa"]), xytext=LABEL_AT[tm], textcoords="data", fontsize=6.8,
                    color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="center",
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.6, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=4))
        continue
    ax.annotate(lab, (r["uc"], r["pa"]), xytext=off_, textcoords="offset points", fontsize=6.8,
                color=style.INK if tm in CORE else style.INK_2, fontweight="bold" if tm in CORE else "normal",
                ha="left" if off_[0] > 0 else "right", va="center")
s24 = FP.loc[(2024, "SEA")]
ax.annotate("", (f25.loc["SEA", "uc"], f25.loc["SEA", "pa"]), xytext=(s24["uc"], s24["pa"]),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (3, 2)),
                            shrinkA=3, shrinkB=6))
ax.annotate("Seattle 2024", (s24["uc"], s24["pa"]), xytext=(0, -9), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=6.4,
            color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="top")
ax.axvline(f25["uc"].median(), color=style.MUTED, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.axhline(f25["pa"].median(), color=style.MUTED, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.text(f25["uc"].median() + 0.004, 0.147, "league median", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="bottom")
ax.text(0.103, f25["pa"].median() + 0.002, "league median", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="bottom")
ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(plt.MultipleLocator(0.05))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlabel("Quarterback under center (share of plays), 2025", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Play-action (share of dropbacks)", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7, handletextpad=0.2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The core of the family is easy to spot in @fig-fingerprint. In 2025 the Rams put Stafford under center on
`{python} pct(FP.loc[(2025, 'LA'), 'uc'])` of their plays, the most in the league, and used play-action on
`{python} pct(FP.loc[(2025, 'LA'), 'pa'])` of dropbacks, also the most. The 49ers were under center on
`{python} pct(FP.loc[(2025, 'SF'), 'uc'])` (`{python} ordinal(int(FP.loc[(2025, 'SF'), 'uc_rk']))`). Seattle
made the most dramatic move of any team in the chart: under center on `{python} pct(FP.loc[(2024, 'SEA'), 'uc'])`
of plays in 2024, `{python} ordinal(int(FP.loc[(2024, 'SEA'), 'uc_rk']))` in the league, and on
`{python} pct(FP.loc[(2025, 'SEA'), 'uc'])` in 2025, `{python} ordinal(int(FP.loc[(2025, 'SEA'), 'uc_rk']))`,
the year Klint Kubiak arrived as offensive coordinator. One new play-caller, and the fingerprint moved across
the whole chart.

Two surprises are worth noticing. The first is San Francisco's play-action rate, which in FTN's charting is
ordinary: `{python} pct(FP.loc[(2025, 'SF'), 'pa'])` of dropbacks in 2025,
`{python} ordinal(int(FP.loc[(2025, 'SF'), 'pa_rk']))` in the league, and in the bottom half in every season
from 2022 to 2025. FTN's play-action flag counts snaps with a fake handoff, and the 49ers fake less than you'd guess:
their "it all looks the same" effect comes less from the fake itself than from the formation, the
personnel and the motion that the runs, the passes and the boots all share. Where the 49ers *are* extreme is
motion (`{python} ordinal(int(FP.loc[(2025, 'SF'), 'motion_rk']))` in 2025,
`{python} ", ".join(ordinal(int(FP.loc[(s, 'SF'), 'motion_rk'])) for s in [2022, 2023])` and
`{python} ordinal(int(FP.loc[(2024, 'SF'), 'motion_rk']))` in the three seasons before) and personnel. The second surprise is how scattered the second generation is: the Bengals
under Zac Taylor are a shotgun passing team, and Atlanta in 2025 was under center less than almost anyone. A
coaching tree hands down a way of thinking and a vocabulary, not a formation chart.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (where 49ers runs ended up, 2019-2025)"
#| output: false
_r = PLAYS[(PLAYS["play_type"] == "run") & (PLAYS["qb_scramble"] != 1) & PLAYS["season"].between(2019, 2025)]
_out = _r.groupby("posteam")["run_gap"].apply(lambda g: g.eq("end").mean())
OUT_SF, OUT_RK, OUT_LG = _out["SF"], int(_out.rank(ascending=False, method="min")["SF"]), _r["run_gap"].eq("end").mean()
```

One thing the fingerprint can't show is how often the 49ers run wide zone. Public play-by-play doesn't
record the blocking scheme, only where the run ended up, and by that measure San Francisco looks ordinary:
`{python} pct(OUT_SF)` of its runs from 2019 to 2025 were charted outside the tackles,
`{python} ordinal(OUT_RK)` in the league, against `{python} pct(OUT_LG)` for the league. That isn't a contradiction.
A wide-zone run is *aimed* outside, but the back cuts wherever the crease is, and a run that bends back inside is
charted as an inside run. The scheme is in the aim, not the destination, which is why the charting services that
grade blocking schemes from film are the only source for it.

The fingerprint has also been *spreading* beyond the tree. League-wide, quarterbacks were under
center on `{python} pct(LG_UC.loc[2023])` of plays in 2023 and `{python} pct(LG_UC.loc[2025])` in 2025 by FTN's
charting, the reversal of a decade-long slide toward the shotgun.[^ftn] Offenses that are not in the tree have
been borrowing its habits.

### YAC over expected

```{python}
#| label: fig-yacoe
#| fig-cap: "YAC over expected, the 49ers' signature. Left: every team's yards after the catch per completion above nflverse's expected YAC, pooled over the 2019–2025 regular seasons; San Francisco (blue) is first by a wide margin. Right: the 49ers season by season, 2017–2025, with their rank among the 32 teams above each bar (nflverse model) and below it in grey the rank by Next Gen Stats' tracking-based model (available from 2018; NGS team values are reception-weighted averages of the receivers it lists). Both models put San Francisco first in most seasons from 2018 to 2023. The 2025 drop came in a season when the receiving corps changed and Mac Jones started about half the games. Data: nflverse play-by-play; NGS receiving via nflreadpy."
ngs = nfl().load_nextgen_stats(seasons=list(range(2018, 2026)), stat_type="receiving").to_pandas()
ngs = ngs[(ngs["week"] == 0) & (ngs["season_type"] == "REG") & ngs["team_abbr"].notna()].copy()
ngs["tot"] = ngs["avg_yac_above_expectation"] * ngs["receptions"]
NGS_T = ngs.groupby(["season", "team_abbr"]).agg(tot=("tot", "sum"), rec=("receptions", "sum")).reset_index()
NGS_T["yacoe"] = NGS_T["tot"] / NGS_T["rec"]
NGS_T["rank"] = NGS_T.groupby("season")["yacoe"].rank(ascending=False).astype(int)
NGS_SF = NGS_T[NGS_T["team_abbr"] == "SF"].set_index("season")["rank"]

POOL = CATCH[CATCH["season"].between(2019, 2025)].groupby("posteam")["yacoe"].mean().sort_values()
SF_SEASONS = list(range(2017, 2026))
sf_y = YR.xs("SF", level="posteam").loc[SF_SEASONS]

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.9), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1, 1.35]))
cols = [style.SERIES[0] if t == "SF" else style.BASELINE for t in POOL.index]
a1.barh(np.arange(len(POOL)), POOL.values, color=cols, height=0.72)
a1.set_yticks(np.arange(len(POOL)), POOL.index, fontsize=6.2)
a1.axvline(0, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8)
a1.set_xlim(-0.85, 1.12)
a1.set_title("All teams, 2019–2025", fontsize=9)
a1.set_xlabel("YAC over expected per catch (yards)", fontsize=7.5)
a1.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
a1.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
a1.annotate(f"{POOL['SF']:+.2f}", (POOL["SF"], len(POOL) - 1), xytext=(-3, 0), textcoords="offset points",
            ha="right", va="center", fontsize=7, color="white", fontweight="bold")
a1.set_ylim(-0.7, len(POOL) - 0.3)

x = np.arange(len(SF_SEASONS))
a2.bar(x, sf_y["yacoe"].values, color=[style.SERIES[0] if v > 0 else style.SERIES[1] for v in sf_y["yacoe"]],
       width=0.66)
a2.axhline(0, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8)
for xi, s, v, rk in zip(x, SF_SEASONS, sf_y["yacoe"].values, sf_y["rank"].values):
    a2.text(xi, v + (0.06 if v >= 0 else -0.06), ordinal(int(rk)), ha="center",
            va="bottom" if v >= 0 else "top", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    ng = f"NGS\n{ordinal(int(NGS_SF[s]))}" if s in NGS_SF.index else "NGS\nn/a"
    a2.text(xi, -1.02, ng, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.2, color=style.MUTED)
a2.set_xticks(x, [str(s) for s in SF_SEASONS], fontsize=7)
a2.set_ylim(-1.25, 2.3)
a2.set_title("49ers by season (rank of 32)", fontsize=9)
a2.set_ylabel("YAC over expected per catch (yards)", fontsize=7.5)
a2.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
a2.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()

NUM1 = int((sf_y.loc[2018:2023, "rank"] == 1).sum())
```

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (the 2021 Deebo Samuel row, which NGS lists without a team)"
#| output: false
_n = nfl().load_nextgen_stats(seasons=list(range(2018, 2026)), stat_type="receiving").to_pandas()
_n = _n[(_n["week"] == 0) & (_n["season_type"] == "REG") & (_n["receptions"] >= 40)]
DEEBO = _n[(_n["player_display_name"] == "Deebo Samuel") & (_n["season"] == 2021)].iloc[0]
DEEBO_RANK = int((_n["avg_yac_above_expectation"] > DEEBO["avg_yac_above_expectation"]).sum()) + 1
REC_MED, REC_P90 = _n["avg_yac_above_expectation"].quantile([0.5, 0.9])
```

No team in the period comes close to San Francisco in @fig-yacoe. From 2019 to 2025 the 49ers' receivers gained
`{python} f"{POOL['SF']:+.2f}"` yards after the catch per reception beyond what nflverse's model expected,
against `{python} f"{POOL.iloc[-2]:+.2f}"` for the next team, `{python} POOL.index[-2]`. They ranked first in
`{python} "every one" if NUM1 == 6 else WORDS[NUM1]` of the six seasons from 2018 to 2023, a stretch that began with C. J. Beathard and Nick Mullens
throwing to Kittle in 2018. Among receivers with 40 or more catches from 2018 to 2025, Deebo Samuel's 2021
ranks `{python} ordinal(DEEBO_RANK)` in Next Gen Stats' YAC over expected:
`{python} f"{DEEBO['avg_yac_above_expectation']:+.1f}"` yards per catch above what the tracking model expected.
For scale: the median receiver-season in that group is `{python} f"{REC_MED:+.1f}"` and one in ten beats
`{python} f"{REC_P90:+.1f}"`, so Samuel's season is an outlier even among individuals. Team numbers are much
smaller because they average every catch by every receiver, the tight end's six-yard out included; a team
half a yard per catch above expectation is very good, and the 49ers' seven-year average was
`{python} f"{POOL['SF']:+.2f}"`.

The two models agreeing matters. nflverse's model doesn't know where the defenders were, so it credits the
49ers for space the *design* created; Next Gen Stats' model does know, and it still ranked them first in most
of those seasons, so their receivers were also doing more with the space than the space alone predicts. Design
and players, together. The 2025 bars are the reminder that YAC is partly personnel: Deebo Samuel was traded to
Washington before the 2025 season, and Mac Jones started about half the games.[^sf25]

### Does it produce points?

All of that would be trivia if the offense weren't good. @fig-epa-rank shows where San Francisco's offense
ranked in EPA per play in each season from 2019 to 2025, with the quarterbacks who took its dropbacks.

```{python}
#| label: fig-epa-rank
#| fig-cap: "San Francisco's offense, EPA per play rank among the 32 teams, 2019–2025 regular seasons (all runs and passes; 1st = most efficient), with the quarterbacks who took the most dropbacks each season beneath (a second name if he took at least a quarter of them). Six of the seven seasons are in the top ten (shaded), with the dropbacks spread across several quarterbacks. The outlier, 2020, was a season of injuries in which three quarterbacks started. Data: nflverse play-by-play."
RANK_SEASONS = list(range(2019, 2026))
sf_rank = [int(RANK[(s, "SF")]) for s in RANK_SEASONS]
sf_epa = [float(TEAM_EPA[(TEAM_EPA["season"] == s) & (TEAM_EPA["posteam"] == "SF")]["epa"].iloc[0]) for s in RANK_SEASONS]
sfd = DROP[(DROP["posteam"] == "SF") & DROP["passer"].notna()]


def qb_line(season):
    c = sfd[sfd["season"] == season]["passer"].value_counts(normalize=True)
    names = [c.index[0]] + [n for n in c.index[1:2] if c[n] >= 0.25]
    return ",\n".join(n.split(".", 1)[1] for n in names)


N_QB = sfd[sfd["season"].isin(RANK_SEASONS)].groupby("season")["passer"].agg(lambda c: c.value_counts().index[0]).nunique()
N_QB_ALL = len({n for s_ in RANK_SEASONS for n in qb_line(s_).replace(",\n", "|").split("|")})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
ax.axhspan(0.5, 10.5, color=style.OFFENSE_TINT, alpha=0.55, zorder=0, lw=0)
ax.text(len(RANK_SEASONS) - 0.62, 10.0, "top ten", fontsize=7, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, va="bottom", ha="right")
x = np.arange(len(RANK_SEASONS))
ax.plot(x, sf_rank, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2, marker="o", ms=8, mec=style.SURFACE, mew=1.5, zorder=3)
for xi, rk, e in zip(x, sf_rank, sf_epa):
    ax.annotate(f"{ordinal(rk)}\n{e:+.2f}", (xi, rk), xytext=(0, 10), textcoords="offset points",
                ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color=style.INK)
ax.set_xticks(x, [f"{s}\n{qb_line(s)}" for s in RANK_SEASONS], fontsize=7)
ax.set_ylim(33, -4)
ax.set_yticks([1, 8, 16, 24, 32])
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per play rank (1 = best)", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Six of seven seasons in the top ten, including first in 2023 (Purdy's league-leading season, with McCaffrey the
Offensive Player of the Year), with `{python} WORDS[N_QB]` different quarterbacks leading the team in dropbacks
along the way and `{python} WORDS[N_QB_ALL]` taking at least a quarter of them in some season. Before
2019 the system was still being built: the 49ers ranked `{python} ordinal(int(RANK[(2017, 'SF')]))` in 2017 and
`{python} ordinal(int(RANK[(2018, 'SF')]))` in 2018, with Hoyer, Beathard, Garoppolo and Mullens all starting
games. That steadiness across passers is the strongest single piece of evidence for the system's claim. It
isn't proof (the 49ers also had elite players at tight end, running back, receiver and left tackle in most
of those seasons), but no other offense of the period stayed this efficient through this much change at
quarterback.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Francisco 49ers 2019"}
**The game:** the NFC Championship Game against Green Bay, January 19, 2020, the purest wide-zone game of
the era. San Francisco won 37–20 while Jimmy Garoppolo threw eight passes (six completions) and was sacked
once. The 49ers ran 42 times for 285 yards, and Raheem Mostert had 220 of them and four touchdowns.[^nfccg]

**What to notice:**

- The same track to both sides. Watch the five linemen's first step and the back's path on run after run: it
  is the same play aimed left, right, and left again, with the fullback (Kyle Juszczyk) leading outside.
- The backside end. Find him on each run: nobody blocks him, and he spends the afternoon chasing from behind.
- How little the offense needed to pass. Eight throws is the system's base play doing all of the work,
  because the defense never made it stop.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Atlanta Falcons 2016"}
**The season:** Kyle Shanahan's second and last as Atlanta's offensive coordinator. The Falcons led the NFL
with 540 points, Matt Ryan was named MVP, and they reached Super Bowl LI, where they led New England 28–3 in
the third quarter and lost 34–28 in the first overtime in Super Bowl history.[^atl16]

**What to notice:**

- This is the system before San Francisco: outside zone with two backs who could both run and catch
  (Devonta Freeman and Tevin Coleman), bootlegs off it, and play-action shots to Julio Jones. The fullback
  ingredient is already here too: Patrick DiMarco made the Pro Bowl after Kyle's first Atlanta season (2015).[^dimarco]
- Watch the running backs as receivers. Much of the Shanahan YAC game in its later 49ers form (the back
  leaking out of the backfield, the screen against a blitz) is already here.
- Watch Ryan's feet on play-action. He turns his back to the defense under center, carries out the fake, and
  throws to a receiver who is already open, often crossing. It is the "easy throw" in action.
- The clip the critics cite. Super Bowl LI, fourth quarter, Atlanta up 28–20 with 3:56 left and the ball on New
  England's 23 after a Julio Jones catch: on second-and-11 Ryan dropped back and was sacked for a 12-yard loss,
  and a holding penalty on the next snap pushed Atlanta out of field-goal range. A field goal would have made it
  a two-score game; New England tied it and won in overtime.[^sb51]
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Miami Dolphins 2023"}
**The season:** Mike McDaniel's second as Miami's head coach. McDaniel spent most of his career on Kyle
Shanahan's staffs (in Houston, Washington, Cleveland, Atlanta and San Francisco, where he was run-game
coordinator and then, in 2021, offensive coordinator) and brought the system to Miami in 2022 with a twist: speed. In Week 3 of 2023 the
Dolphins beat Denver 70–20; Tua Tagovailoa led the league with 4,624 passing yards and Tyreek Hill had 1,799
receiving yards.[^mia23]

**What to notice:**

- Motion on almost every snap, much of it at the snap, the most of any team in the league (by FTN's charting
  Miami was first in motion in 2022, 2023 and 2025). Three weeks into 2023, ESPN's tracking had Miami with a
  man in motion *at* the snap on 59% of plays, the highest rate for any team since ESPN began counting in 2017.[^motion]
- The fullback. Miami was the league leader in 21 personnel in 2022 and 2023 by nflverse's data, with Alec
  Ingold leading wide zone and slicing on boots, but Miami's backs and receivers were sprinters, so the same
  ideas produced longer plays.
- The limit. The Dolphins' offense faded late in 2023 and fell to the bottom half of the league in EPA per play
  in 2024 and 2025, and McDaniel was fired in January 2026. A system can raise a team's floor; it doesn't
  guarantee a ceiling, and it doesn't protect a coach.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams 2018 and 2025"}
**The seasons:** two versions of Sean McVay's offense, seven years apart. In 2018 the Rams went 13–3 and reached
Super Bowl LIII with Jared Goff, running the whole offense out of one personnel group (11 personnel on about
93% of plays, [08-02](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd)'s film room). In 2025,
with Matthew Stafford at 37, the Rams were first in the league in both under-center rate and play-action rate
and second in EPA per play, and Stafford was MVP.

**What to do:** watch one game from each. In 2018 count the snaps in 11 personnel and notice how much of the
deception comes from receivers' splits and motion, not substitutions; that is McVay's answer to the personnel
problem the 49ers solved with a fullback. In 2025 watch the play-action passes from under center and see how quickly
Stafford's eyes come back downfield after the fake and the ball comes out on the first hitch of his drop. Then compare the two
quarterbacks on third-and-long: that is the debate from earlier, on film.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seattle Seahawks 2025"}
**The season:** Klint Kubiak's only year as Seattle's offensive coordinator, under defensive head coach Mike
Macdonald, ending in Super Bowl LX: Seattle 29, New England 13. Kenneth Walker III ran 27 times for 135 yards and
was the game's MVP.[^sblx]

**What to notice:**

- The fingerprint on film. Seattle went from the bottom third of the league in under-center rate in 2024 to
  near the top in 2025 (@fig-fingerprint), and in the Super Bowl the quarterback was under center on about half
  the snaps, as he had been all year.
- Wide zone as the base play, with Walker as the one-cut back: press the aiming point, cut once, go.
- The pairing. When Seattle has run from a look two or three times, watch the backside end on the next snap
  from it; that is when the boot and the play-action come. Seattle's 2025 quarterback was Sam Darnold
  (see @fig-same-qb).
:::

## The tree in 2025 and 2026

A [coaching tree](12-01-walsh-49ers-west-coast.qmd) is the family of coaches descended from one head coach,
traced through who worked on whose staff. [The Walsh case study](12-01-walsh-49ers-west-coast.qmd) draws the
whole Walsh tree, of which this family is the largest modern branch: Mike Shanahan was Seifert's coordinator
in San Francisco before he went to Denver. This section zooms in on the part of it that calls plays today.

The family has two roots in the Denver building of the 1990s. Gary Kubiak, Mike Shanahan's coordinator, carried
the system to Houston as head coach (2006–13) and back to Denver, where he won Super Bowl 50 after the 2015
season; his sons Klint and Klay are coaches in it now. Kyle Shanahan took it through Houston, Washington,
Cleveland and Atlanta to San Francisco. The decisive moment was the Washington staff of 2010–13, under Mike
Shanahan with Kyle as offensive coordinator: Sean McVay coached the tight ends, Matt LaFleur the quarterbacks,
and Mike McDaniel (from 2011) was an offensive assistant and then the receivers coach. All four became NFL head coaches.[^was] (That Washington offense
also produced one of the scheme's purest seasons: in 2012 Alfred Morris, a sixth-round rookie, ran for 1,613
yards in wide zone, beside rookie quarterback Robert Griffin III and the read-option plays the staff borrowed
from Baylor, which [The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd) covers.)[^morris]

From there it branched. McVay's own staffs in Los Angeles produced head coaches Zac Taylor (Bengals, 2019),
Kevin O'Connell (Vikings, 2022) and Liam Coen (Jaguars, 2025). LaFleur took the system to Green Bay in 2019;
Aaron Rodgers won two MVPs in it. Kyle's 49ers staffs produced McDaniel (Dolphins, 2022), Mike LaFleur (Matt's
brother) and Brian Fleury, and they gave Klint Kubiak a season on the staff before he went on to run offenses in
New Orleans and Seattle.

Staffs change every winter, and this one changed a lot. @fig-staff-moves lays out who held which job in the
2025 season and the 2026 season.

```{python}
#| label: fig-staff-moves
#| fig-cap: "Recent staff moves: the Shanahan family's play-callers and coordinators, 2025 season vs 2026 season (staffs as of October 2026). Each row is one coach; the left card is his 2025 job, the right card his 2026 job (OC: offensive coordinator). Orange cards changed over the winter. 'Calls plays' marks the coach who called his offense's plays that season; it is left off where the coach didn't call them (Stefanski handed Cleveland's play-calling to Tommy Rees during 2025, and Rees calls Atlanta's in 2026) or where no report confirms who does. The family lost a head coach in Miami and gained three, in Las Vegas, Arizona and Atlanta; Miami's offense stays in the family under Slowik, and Seattle replaced one family play-caller with another."
# (coach, how he joined the family, 2025 job, 2026 job, calls plays 2025, calls plays 2026)
MOVES = [
    ("Kyle Shanahan", "Mike Shanahan's son; Kubiak's Texans", "49ers head coach", "49ers head coach", True, True),
    ("Klay Kubiak", "Gary Kubiak's son, Klint's brother", "49ers OC", "49ers OC", False, False),
    ("Brian Fleury", "49ers staff 2019–25", "49ers run-game coordinator & TEs", "Seahawks OC", False, True),
    ("Klint Kubiak", "Gary Kubiak's son, Klay's brother", "Seahawks OC", "Raiders head coach", True, True),
    ("Mike McDaniel", "Kyle's staffs, Houston to SF", "Dolphins head coach", "Chargers OC", True, True),
    ("Bobby Slowik", "49ers 2017–22; Texans OC 2023–24", "Dolphins senior pass-game coordinator", "Dolphins OC", False, False),
    ("Kevin Stefanski", "Vikings OC 2019, Gary Kubiak advising", "Browns head coach", "Falcons head coach", False, False),
    ("Sean McVay", "Washington staff 2010–16", "Rams head coach", "Rams head coach", True, True),
    ("Mike LaFleur", "Kyle's staffs; Matt's brother", "Rams OC", "Cardinals head coach", False, True),
    ("Matt LaFleur", "Washington, Atlanta; McVay's OC 2017", "Packers head coach", "Packers head coach", True, True),
    ("Kevin O'Connell", "McVay's OC 2020–21", "Vikings head coach", "Vikings head coach", True, True),
    ("Liam Coen", "McVay's Rams staffs", "Jaguars head coach", "Jaguars head coach", True, True),
    ("Zac Taylor", "McVay's Rams 2017–18", "Bengals head coach", "Bengals head coach", True, True),
    ("Nick Caley", "from McVay's Rams staff", "Texans OC", "Texans OC", True, False),
]
W, H = 6.6, 0.34 * len(MOVES) + 0.75
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(W, H))
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
ax.set_xlim(0, W); ax.set_ylim(0, H); ax.axis("off")
X_NAME, X25, X26, CW, CH = 0.06, 1.84, 4.26, 2.28, 0.27
ax.text(X25 + CW / 2, H - 0.2, "2025 season", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold",
        color=style.INK)
ax.text(X26 + CW / 2, H - 0.2, "2026 season", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold",
        color=style.INK)
ax.text(X_NAME, H - 0.2, "Coach (how he joined the family)", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=7.6,
        fontweight="bold", color=style.INK_2)
for i, (name, root, j25, j26, c25, c26) in enumerate(MOVES):
    y = H - 0.55 - i * 0.34
    changed = j25 != j26
    ax.text(X_NAME, y + 0.055, name, fontsize=7.4, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center")
    ax.text(X_NAME, y - 0.085, root, fontsize=5.8, color=style.INK_2, va="center")
    for xc, job, calls, hot in [(X25, j25, c25, False), (X26, j26, c26, changed)]:
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((xc, y - CH / 2), CW, CH, boxstyle="round,pad=0.01,rounding_size=0.05",
                                    fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT if hot else style.SURFACE,
                                    ec=style.DEFENSE if hot else style.BASELINE, lw=1.1 if hot else 0.7))
        ax.text(xc + 0.07, y, job, fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, va="center",
                fontweight="bold" if hot else "normal")
        if calls:
            ax.text(xc + CW - 0.07, y, "calls plays", fontsize=5.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, va="center",
                    ha="right", style="italic")
    ax.annotate("", (X26 - 0.03, y), xytext=(X25 + CW + 0.03, y),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.DEFENSE if changed else style.BASELINE, lw=0.9))
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-staff-moves with the season labels in mind, because the two lists are easy to blur.

**In the 2025 season** the family's play-callers ran the 49ers (Kyle Shanahan), the Rams (McVay, with Mike
LaFleur as offensive coordinator), the Packers (Matt LaFleur), the Dolphins (McDaniel), the Seahawks (Klint
Kubiak, as offensive coordinator under defensive head coach Mike Macdonald), and, a generation down, the
Vikings, Jaguars and Bengals, plus coordinators from McVay's staffs calling plays in Atlanta and Houston. The season ended with the family everywhere: the NFC Championship Game was Seattle
against the Rams, 31–27, and Seattle went on to win Super Bowl LX 29–13 over New England.[^lx]

**In the 2026 season** the map is different. Miami fired McDaniel in January and he became the Chargers'
offensive coordinator and play-caller; Klint Kubiak became the Raiders' head coach after his one season in
Seattle and kept calling plays; Mike LaFleur left the Rams to become the Cardinals' head coach and calls their
plays; Seattle replaced Kubiak with Brian Fleury, the 49ers' run-game coordinator and tight ends coach, so the
Seahawks stayed in the family. Miami's offense did too: the new head coach, Jeff Hafley, is a defensive coach, and
his offensive coordinator is Bobby Slowik, who spent 2017–22 on Kyle Shanahan's staffs and 2025 on McDaniel's. A
third branch runs through Gary Kubiak himself: Kevin Stefanski called the 2019 Vikings' plays with Kubiak beside
him as adviser, the season Kubiak's zone scheme came to Minnesota, coached Cleveland from 2020 to 2025, and is
Atlanta's head coach in 2026. In San Francisco, Shanahan still calls the plays with Klay Kubiak as offensive
coordinator, in Los Angeles Nathan Scheelhaase was promoted to replace Mike LaFleur, and in Houston Nick Caley is
still the coordinator.[^staffs] Whether the 2026 branches are working is too early to say; this chapter's data
stops with the 2025 season.

The lesson of the moves board is how the system *spreads*: not by teams copying film, but by assistants
leaving with the playbook and the vocabulary in their heads. That is also why the family's offenses differ. A
coordinator who leaves takes the ideas, but he builds them around his own quarterback, his own roster and his
own instincts, which is how a shotgun team in Cincinnati and an under-center team in Los Angeles can share a
grandfather.

## How defenses answered

A system this successful for this long gets studied by every defensive staff in the league. Their answers
fall into four groups, and you will see all four on any Sunday.

**1. Change the front.** The bear in @fig-bear-wide-zone is the oldest answer: cover the interior linemen
so nobody can climb. Its cousin is the [tite front](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd)
(a nose and two linemen on the tackles' inside shoulders), which walls off the middle and asks the edges to
win; and its opposite is a *wide* four-man front with a quick 3-technique who penetrates before the guard's reach
can land ([05-01](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd) animates it).
[Odd and Hybrid Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd) explains why no
single front stops both zone runs, so defenses change fronts by opponent and by down. The offense's counter is
everything in this chapter: the fullback, the unblocked backside end and the boot, and the change-ups from the
bear section (split zone, crack-toss, duo and counter) out of the same looks when the front is built for zone.

**2. Keep two safeties deep and play the run with fewer men.** The most important defensive trend of the
2020s, the [two-high](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) shell, is partly an
answer to this family. Play-action and bootlegs work best against a defense that brings a safety down to stop
the run, so defenses led by Vic Fangio and his descendants kept both safeties deep, accepted a
[light box](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd), and trusted bigger fronts
to hold up against the run. Two-high coverage rose from 32.9% of snaps in 2018 to 42.0% in 2025 by Next Gen
Stats' count, the highest since tracking began.[^twohigh] The fight between that idea and this one is the subject
of [Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd), and of
[The Modern Era](../11-history/11-05-the-modern-era.qmd).

**3. Take away the middle and make the quarterback hold the ball.** The crossing routes that produce all that
YAC run through the middle of the field at linebacker depth. Fill that area with defenders, rush with
stunts that take a moment to develop, and the quarterback who wanted to throw to a receiver on the move is
holding the ball. The most famous example is New England's plan in Super Bowl LIII, which held McVay's Rams to 3
points; [The Belichick case study](12-02-belichick-patriots-game-plan.qmd) draws it.

**4. Hunt the tells.** An offense built on looking the same can be beaten if it *doesn't* quite look the same.
Defensive staffs grade the running back's depth, the fullback's alignment, the receivers' splits and the
direction of the motion, looking for any detail that separates the run from the boot. That is the self-scouting
war of [08-02](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd): the offense's job is to keep
its tendencies balanced inside each look, and the defense's job is to find the one look that isn't.

And the system answered back. When defenses went light and two-high, the family ran the ball more and got
heavier (in 2025 offenses used fewer than three wide receivers on 41.7% of plays, the highest rate in the Next
Gen Stats era), and when the bear came, the boots came with it.[^heavy] When defenses took away the
crossers, McVay went and got a quarterback who could beat them from the pocket.

## What survives

Ideas from this family are now just *how offense is played* in much of the NFL, including by teams with no
connection to it:

- **Under center is back,** led by this family (the numbers are in the fingerprint section).
- **Motion is universal.** PFF counted a shift or motion on 63.9% of plays in 2025, up from 38.4% in 2016;
  every team but one used it on at least half its plays.[^pff]
- **Heavier personnel is back,** for the same reason the 49ers kept a fullback: to make light defenses pay.
- **YAC as a design goal.** Receivers are now scouted and drafted for what they do after the catch, and
  offenses design throws to catch them on the move.
- **The illusion of complexity** (few plays, many looks; many plays, one look) is standard teaching on almost
  every offensive staff, inside the tree and out.

What may not survive is the specific balance. The 2025 Rams leaned harder on play-action from under center
than anyone, while the 49ers' play-action rate was ordinary, and the 2025 second generation in Cincinnati and Atlanta
looks more like a spread offense than like Denver in 1998. A tree spreads by mutating. That is also how you will
know it is still alive: the family resemblance will be in the questions the offense asks a defense, not in any
one formation.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**On Sunday: same look, different plays.** Pick one Shanahan-family offense (in 2026: the 49ers, Rams,
Packers, Vikings, Jaguars, Bengals, Texans, the Seahawks under Fleury, the Raiders under Klint Kubiak, the
Cardinals under Mike LaFleur, the Chargers under McDaniel, the Dolphins under Slowik or the Falcons under
Stefanski) and keep a simple chart for one half.

*Before each snap*

- Write the **look**: personnel (count the backs and tight ends), where the quarterback is (under center or
  shotgun), and the **motion** (none, across, jet, orbit). For example, "21, under center, Z across."
- Is there a **fullback**? If so, where is he: offset to the tight end (the base look) or away from it? A
  fullback's alignment is one of the tells defensive staffs grade, so when it changes, note what follows.

*In the first second*

- Do all five linemen step the same way? (Zone.) Does the back run toward the tight end? (Wide zone, or a fake of it.)
- Find the **backside end** and watch him. Does he chase the back, or stay home?

*After the play*

- Write what the play turned out to be: wide zone, gap run, bootleg, keeper, play-action shot, dropback.
- If it was a pass, where was the receiver when he caught it: **moving or standing**, and with how much space
  ahead? That is YAC by design.

*At halftime*

- For each look, list the different plays run from it. A good Shanahan-family half has several plays from each
  look; a look that produced only one play is a tendency the defense can find (and so can you). When a look has
  produced a run or two and the backside end has been chasing, start watching for the bootleg from that look.

A template:

| Look (personnel, alignment, motion) | Plays seen | Backside end |
|---|---|---|
| 21, under center, Z across | wide zone R, wide zone R, boot L | chased twice |
| 11, gun, jet from left | jet sweep, play-action cross | stayed home |
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1.** First-and-10 from your own 35, third quarter. The offense is in 21 personnel, the quarterback under
center, the fullback offset to the tight end, who is lined up on the **left** this time. The defense shows the bear
again: the center and both guards covered, eight in the box, one deep safety. On the offense's last three wide-zone
runs toward the tight end, the backside end (on the **right**, ringed) crashed hard down the line after the back,
and one of those runs lost two yards anyway. What is the offense's best call, and which way will it go?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: 21 personnel, offset I, the tight end on the left; a bear front with the strong safety in the box and one deep safety. The backside end (ringed) is on the offense's right."
p = Play(off21(strength="left"), bear(s=-1), los=35, to_go=10)
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-13.5, 13.5), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A bootleg to the right (the side away from the tight end), probably naked, with the keeper built in.** Wide zone
here goes left, toward the tight end, so the play's backside is the offense's right, where the end has been
crashing. Three runs have taught him to chase, and he is the defender the offense leaves unblocked against the
bear. The quarterback fakes wide zone left, keeps the ball and rolls right behind him: the fullback slices into
the right flat, the tight end crosses from left to right behind the linebackers who flowed with the fake, and if
nobody comes up to stop him, the quarterback runs. First-and-10 is the ideal down for it: the defense expects run,
and a short completion keeps the offense on schedule.

*Why not run wide zone again?* Against the bear it was losing yards; the defense has the numbers. The offense's
answer is not to block the bear better but to punish the habit the bear's backside end has fallen into.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2.** Second-and-6, early in the first quarter. The offense has one back and one tight end (11
personnel), the tight end in-line on the left, the quarterback under center and the receivers in tight splits
(lined up 9–10 yards from the ball, well inside the numbers, instead of out near the sideline).
Before the snap the Z, a slot receiver on the right, goes in jet motion from right to left (dashed). The defense keeps **two** deep safeties and nobody runs across with the
motion; there are six defenders in the box. Run or pass, and which way?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: 11 personnel under center, the Y in-line on the left, receivers in tight splits (H, the third receiver, and X about 10 yards from the ball); the Z, a slot receiver on the right, goes in jet motion to the left (the dashed arrow ends where he will be at the snap, just behind the quarterback). The defense: a four-man front (a 9 outside the Y, a 3, a 1 and a 5) and two linebackers in the box, a nickel back (NB) who stays outside where the Z started, two cornerbacks and two deep safeties. Nobody follows the motion."
off = named_line(offense("singleback"))
SPOTS = {"Y": (-0.7, -4.8), "H": (-1.5, -10.0), "X": (-0.7, 10.5), "Z": (-1.5, 7.2)}   # Y on the left
off = [q.moved(d=SPOTS[q.key][0], w=SPOTS[q.key][1]) if q.key in SPOTS else
       (q.moved(label="R") if q.key == "RB" else q) for q in off]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.7, "9"), D("LT3", "DT", 1.0, -technique("3"), "3"),
       D("RT1", "DT", 1.0, technique("1"), "1"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5"), "5"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, -1.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, 2.4, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.5, 7.8, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -10.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 10.5, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -6.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 6.5, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=6)
p.motion("Z", to=(-2.6, 1.6))
f = draw(p, lateral=(-14.0, 14.0), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A run.** Count the box: six defenders against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end), with both safeties
12 yards deep. That is a [light box](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd), and the
system's standing answer to two-high safeties is to run the ball at them. The motion told the quarterback two more
things: nobody ran across with the Z, so the coverage is very likely zone, and the safeties didn't rotate down, so
the box is staying light.

Which way is the play-caller's choice, and both answers are textbook in this family:

- **Wide zone left, toward the motion (or the jet sweep itself, handed to the Z).** The Z is just behind the
  quarterback at the snap and keeps running through the mesh toward the left sideline. He doesn't block anyone;
  he is a threat, and the defender on the left edge has to respect a jet sweep for a beat, which is a beat he
  isn't attacking the run.
- **Fake the jet, wide zone right, away from it.** The fake drags the Will and the nickel back toward the motion
  and thins the right side, where the run is going.

If you said "run," you read the picture; the direction is the bonus question.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3.** First-and-10, a series after the bootleg in Drill 1 went for 22 yards. Same 21-personnel look,
tight end on the left, quarterback under center. The defense has changed two things. It now shows **two** deep
safeties before the snap, and when the Z goes in motion across the formation to the right, one safety spins down
into the box on that side while the other runs to the middle of the field. And the backside end on the right is
no longer chasing: on the last two runs he squeezed down the line, square, with his eyes on the quarterback. The
offense's last two wide-zone runs gained 3 and 2 yards. What should the offense call?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: the same 21-personnel look, the Z in motion across to the right (dashed blue). Before the snap the defense shows two deep safeties; as the Z moves, the right-side safety spins down into the box and the other rotates to the deep middle (dashed orange), leaving eight in the box and one deep safety still moving at the snap. The backside end (ringed) squeezes with his eyes on the quarterback."
off3 = off21(strength="left")
d3 = [q.moved(d=12.5, w=8.5) if q.key == "SS" else (q.moved(d=12.5, w=-8.5) if q.key == "FS" else q)
      for q in bear(s=-1)]
p = Play(off3, d3, los=35, to_go=10)
p.motion("Z", to=(-1.5, 6.6))
p.drop("SS", (5.4, 6.6), label=None)
p.drop("FS", (14.0, 0.0), label=None)
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-13.5, 13.5), window=(-9.0, 16.5))
say(f, p, 9.0, 10.6, "spins down\non the motion", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 14.0, -4.6, "rotates to\nthe middle", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, -3.4, 9.2, "squeezes,\neyes on the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A play-action shot from under center, with max protection: two deep routes against the one safety.** Put
the two changes together. The naked boot is off the table, because the end who used to chase is squeezing and
would be waiting for the quarterback. Wide zone is running into eight in the box, which is what the spin was
for. But the spin has a price: one safety is left to cover the whole deep field, and at the snap he is still
running to the middle. That is the picture the
[yankee](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yankee) concept from
[04-05](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) is built for: fake wide zone, keep the
fullback and the back in to protect, and send two receivers deep, a post from one side and a deep over from the
other. The linebackers and the safety who came down step up for the fake; the lone deep safety can take only one
of the two routes, and the quarterback throws the other.

*Why not the protected boot?* It's a fine safe call, and a good one on second-and-long. But it attacks the short
and middle areas the eight-man box is already crowding; on first-and-10 with one deep safety still moving, the
shot is the bigger reward. This back-and-forth, base play, constraint, a new answer, a new constraint, is
[sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd), and it is how a Shanahan
play-caller spends a game.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Two problems, one family.** Gibbs's and Mike Shanahan's 1990s Broncos built wide zone and the bootleg to block
  defenses that never stood still; Kyle Shanahan's 2017 49ers added the fullback, motion and YAC passing to beat
  fast, light defenses without a star quarterback.
- **Four ingredients, one picture.** Wide zone moves the defense sideways, the fullback forces a personnel choice,
  motion makes the defense answer first, and YAC passes throw into the space all of that empties. The same few
  looks carry all of it.
- **Leave a man free on purpose, then punish him.** Against a bear front the offense can't block everyone, so it
  leaves the backside end and beats him with the bootleg-keeper when he crashes; when he squeezes, the cutback,
  split zone and the protected boot are waiting. The defense's answer to the base play sets up the constraint play.
- **The system raises the quarterback's floor, and the ceiling is still argued.** Several quarterbacks were much
  more efficient inside the family than outside it; even the 49ers' third-and-long success is designed. Goff
  thrived in a cousin offense in Detroit, and EPA can't see the difference McVay paid for in Stafford: the
  plays after the design breaks are a coach's judgment, not a number.
- **The fingerprint:** under center and in motion, 21 or heavy personnel (49ers), play-action at the top of the
  league (Rams), and receivers who gain far more after the catch than the catch predicts. From 2019 to 2025 the
  49ers were first in YAC over expected by a wide margin and top ten in EPA per play in six of seven seasons.
- **Label every staff by season.** In 2025 the family's first generation called plays in San Francisco, Los
  Angeles, Green Bay, Miami and Seattle (Super Bowl LX champions), with McVay's former assistants calling them in
  Minnesota, Jacksonville, Cincinnati, Atlanta and Houston. In 2026 Kubiak (Las Vegas) and Mike LaFleur (Arizona)
  are head coaches who call plays, McDaniel calls the Chargers' plays, Fleury Seattle's, Slowik coordinates Miami's
  offense and Stefanski is Atlanta's head coach.
